title: Finally Made a Little Robot Desk Figure I'm Actually Happy With
author: Weird_Cockroach_5928
selftext:
I've been wanting to make a small desk ornament for a while. Recently, I came across a robot design I really liked and thought it would be fun to turnit into a 3D model and print it myself.

I don't have much 3D modeling experience, so I decided to try image to 3D by AI tools. I used meshy's Image to 3D to generate the first version from my reference image. The result was actually better than I expected. The robot's head, body proportions, and overall silhouette were pretty close to the original design.

However, when I rotated the model and checked it from different angles, I noticed that some details on the arms and back hadn't come through quite right. It looked good from the front, but there were some noticeable differences from other angles.

I went back and looked at my reference image again. The background was a bit cluttered, and some of the details weren't very clear. I used Remove Background to clean up the image before preparing it again. This made me realize that the quality of the input image really does affect the generation process, especially for parts that aren't clearly visible in the original reference.

After that, I tried meshy 7 Multi-View feature and added reference images from a few different angles. I was much happier with the result this time, especially the side and back details, which were closer to what I had in mind. Of course, I still needed to make a few adjustments, but at least I didn't have to model everything from scratch.

I think it depends on what you're trying to make. For simple objects with clear shapes, a single image might be enough. But for robots, characters, or models withmore complex structures, adding references from different angles can be much more helpful. After all, one image can only show you so much.

That said, I haven't found an AI 3D generation tool that gives me a model I can send straight to the printer without any preparation. I still need to check the geometry, thin sections, and whether the details are suitable for actual printing. As someone who's still learning 3D modeling, AI has definitely made it much easier for me to try making my own little models.

For those of you who regularly print AI-generated 3D models, what do you usually check or fix before sending them to the printer?
